items.title: Armand Hug Interview, 1976-02-13
items.q: Eddie Miller played there with me for a while.

ctx.x: Why, sure. That's what I told somebody the other night. I said, you know, I said, you know, officially it may have closed down. I said, but don't kid yourself that there wasn't a lot of it still in existence. Even when I was about maybe, say, 12 or 13 years old, when I used to go around walking around on Basin Street, I can remember Eddie Miller and I and Shockey and Julian Lane, or I could have mentioned many musicians that we used to go around there, and we used to encounter lots of the girls, you know, like…
Well, most people don't realize that a lot of it was there. You know, where charity is now.

items.title: Armand Hug Interview, 1960-07-14
items.q: That was the first time I'd ever played with Eddie. ... I played with him with the Owls Orchestra, you know. ... That's when Eddie Miller was playing with them.

ctx.x: Back to the piano players, are there any others that you remember in that era that were outstanding?

Well, I would say that after I began playing around the suburban movie houses in town, I used to play for silent movies in those days. Played with three pieces. We used to get a dollar a piece a night. We didn't even get our call fair, but I was playing with a violin player by the name of Grasshoff and a drummer, Surpass I believe was his name. We used to go down to the St. Maurice Avenue Theater and play for these silent movies. The silent movies got a bad deal in those days because we were playing Tiger Rag or…
Would he sit down at the piano?
